opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a bit of a strange position to be in, isn't it? I'm one of the people whose name is on that paper, and I've had a front-row seat to how much the field has changed since then. But that success has a downside. There's now an enormous amount of talent, money and attention going into one architecture, and the research has become fairly narrow. You get a lot of people making small tweaks: a slightly different normalization, a different positional encoding, a new attention variant. Then they report half a point on some benchmark. That's useful work, but it isn't where I think the interesting breakthroughs will come from.

Honestly, I was getting a bit bored of it. I deliberately decided to cut back on the amount of Transformer research I do. Partly that's because I don't think I have much of a comparative advantage there anymore. Thousands of very smart people are already doing it. And partly it's because I think the field is somewhat stuck in a local minimum. The Transformer works so well that it sucks all the oxygen out of the room. If someone comes along with a genuinely different idea, it has to beat a heavily optimized Transformer on day one, or nobody pays attention. That's a really hard bar for a new idea to clear.

So at Sakana, a big part of what we're trying to do is give ourselves the freedom to explore. We're looking at things inspired by nature, evolution, collective intelligence, and different ways of thinking about computation and time inside a model. Some of it will fail, and that's fine. When we were working on the Transformer, it wasn't an obvious, safe bet either. It came out of a lot of freedom and a bit of playing around. I'd like to get back to that kind of research, rather than adding to the pile of incremental improvements on something that already works.

r001.rationale: He says Transformer research draws enormous talent, money, and attention and has become narrow, contributing to his decision to cut back.

r002.rationale: He frames cutting back as freeing time and room to explore other directions, including nature inspired ideas, evolution, collective intelligence, and alternative computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, part of it is just that I've been staring at this architecture for a very long time now. I was there at the beginning, and I've watched the whole field pile onto it to the point where it feels like almost everybody is doing a slightly different flavor of the same thing. There's a lot of excellent work there, but when you have that many smart people with that much compute all pushing in the same direction, I'm not convinced my marginal contribution is very high anymore. The incremental gains are going to get found with or without me.

The other part is more philosophical. I think the Transformer's success has actually become a bit of a problem for the field. It works so well that it's hard to get anything else funded, published, or even taken seriously. When we built it, it wasn't obvious it would work. We had the freedom to try something that looked weird. That kind of freedom is what I think is missing right now, because everyone is optimizing against a benchmark that's defined by the thing we already have.

And personally, I find that a little boring. I'm much more interested in the questions where nobody knows the answer yet. What would a system that learns more like a living thing look like? Can you get intelligence to emerge from simpler components interacting, rather than one giant monolithic model trained end to end? Those are much riskier bets, and most of them probably won't pan out, but that's exactly the kind of research I think we need more of. If I'm going to spend the next ten years on something, I'd rather it be a long shot that could actually change the picture than another two percent on a leaderboard.

So it's not that I think the Transformer is wrong or finished. It's more that I feel I've done my part there, and the most useful thing I can do now is go look somewhere the crowd isn't.

r001.rationale: He says almost everyone is pursuing variations of the Transformer and that his marginal contribution is low, expressing a perception that the research area is oversaturated.

r002.rationale: He says he would rather pursue risky, unexplored questions and research outside the crowd, presenting reduced Transformer work as a chance to explore other directions.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s easy to get stuck working on the thing you’re known for. You have some success with an idea, and then there’s this pull to keep improving it. But I’d rather give myself room to find something different, even if that means spending time on ideas that don’t work.

There are already so many people working on Transformers. The question for me is where I can contribute something new. If I spend all my time thinking about how to improve the Transformer, I’m implicitly assuming that the Transformer is the right starting point. I want to be able to question that assumption.

r001.rationale: He says there are already many people working on Transformers, framing the area as crowded and helping explain why he wants to redirect his effort.

r002.rationale: He says he wants room to find something different and to question whether the Transformer is the right starting point, presenting reduced focus as a chance to explore other directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Transformer is a very good idea, but it’s still just one idea. When so much of the field is working on the same architecture, I think there’s more value in stepping back and asking what else might work. Otherwise, we risk getting very good at improving Transformers without finding the thing that comes after them.

For me, the exciting part of research is trying something that might fail, but might also give us a fundamentally different way of thinking about the problem. That’s where I’d like to spend more of my time.

r001.rationale: The response says much of the field is working on the same architecture and describes that as a reason to step back from Transformer research.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says he wants to spend more time exploring what else might work and pursuing fundamentally different ways of thinking.
